Sea pig or seapig may refer to:


== Animals ==
Scotoplanes, a genus of deep-sea holothurians (sea cucumbers) commonly called sea pigs
An obsolete name for the Eastern smooth boxfish
Sea Swine (a.k.a. Porcus Marinus), a historical name for porpoise and mythical creatures
A local name for the dugong
The name of guinea pigs in some countries
Hawaiian flagtail, sometimes called puaʻa kai (sea pig)

# Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs Date: November 19, 2026 Source: University of Tokyo Summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery. Share: Deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor. Now, researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered that these unusual animals are hiding something even stranger beneath their "skin." Living within their body walls is a previously unknown bacterium with an extraordinarily small genome and a surprising collection of genes responsible for producing enormous proteins. The researchers identified the bacterium, which they named *Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola*, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues. Genetic analysis revealed that its genome contains just 649,000 DNA bases, yet more than a quarter of its genetic material is devoted to producing groups of proteins associated with the bacterial surface. Some of these "giant" proteins contain more than 5,000 amino acids and may help the bacteria interact with their hosts or form clusters (clustering into groups). The discovery offers new insights into how bacteria adapt to living in close association with other organisms and which biological functions they retain as they become increasingly dependent on their hosts. **Meet the Strange Sea Pigs of the Deep Ocean** Sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known. These small, gelatinous creatures are actually a type of sea cucumber that inhabits the deep ocean. Using numerous tube-shaped feet, they slowly travel across the seafloor, gathering decaying organic material and delivering it to their mouths with specialized tentacles. Despite th

The animals commonly known as sea pigs are in fact a type of sea cucumber. Sea cucumbers are echinoderms, a group of marine animals that includes sea urchins and starfish. Sea pigs are found in all the world's oceans. In some areas, they comprise more than 95% of the total weight of animals on the deep-sea floor. Despite their abundance, most people will never see a sea pig, as they live in the coldest and deepest parts of the ocean. It's a shame, because these little piggies are both cute and play an essential role in the ocean ecosystem. **1. "Sea Pig" is a pretty accurate description.** Sea pigs earned their moniker from their puffy legs and plump, oval-shaped pinkish bodies. **2. They fit in the palm of your hand.** Sea pigs tend to be about 4-6 inches long. **3. Sea pigs live in the deepest part of the ocean.** Sea pigs are found in the deepest abyssal depths of the world's oceans, as far as 3.7 miles under the ocean surface. **4. Scientists have known about sea pigs for more than 100 years.** They were first described by Swedish zoologist Hjalmar Théel in 1882. Théel described about 65 new species discovered by the British research ship HMS *Challenger* during her round-the-world expedition of 1872-1876. **5. They get around by walking on the seafloor.** Sea pigs have five to seven pairs of enlarged tube feet. These "walking legs" are hydraulically operated appendages that can be inflated and deflated to move around. **6. Those aren't antennae — they're also feet.** Although they look like antennae, the structures on the top of the sea pig's head are actually feet. These upper papillae are modified tube feet, like the animal's "walking legs." They may help propel the sea pig along the ocean, or they may have a sensory function, helping it detect the chemical trail of a tasty meal. **7. Sea pigs scour mud for delicious scum.** Sea pigs are deposit or detrital feeders, eating bits of decaying plant and animal material found in deep sea mud. Their mouths are surrounded by a ring of feeding tentacles that they use to sift through the mud and grab onto food. Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked trusted source proofread In the deep ocean, translucent sea pigs trundle across the seafloor. Researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered an unusual bacterium beneath the sea pig's "skin." Through fluorescent imaging, they determined the location of the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola. DNA analysis revealed a minimized genome of just 649,000 bases. Unexpectedly, more than a quarter of this was dedicated to building surface-associated protein groups, including "giant" proteins exceeding 5,000 amino acids in length, possibly for interactions with host tissues or bacterial aggregation (clustering into groups). This study, published in the journal *ISME Host Microbe*, offers clues to which functions remain in symbiotic bacteria living closely with their host. ## Sea pigs shelter more than crabs The sea pig is a small, jellylike creature that lives in the deep ocean and is a type of sea cucumber. It slowly meanders across the ocean floor on its many tubelike feet, scooping up dead matter into its tentacled mouth. It may be small, but it is influential in the ocean ecosystem. Not only does it recycle organic matter and nutrients, but, despite its defenseless appearance, its squishy body provides shelter from predators to young king crabs. However, there is a lot we don't know about these curious-looking creatures. How long do they live? Why do they have waving, antennalike protrusions on their heads?
